--- title: "Three time axes" jupyter: coi-docs --- Every measure in the lake carries three distinct notions of "when," and conflating them is the characteristic error in this domain. | Axis | Column(s) | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | **Period** | `period_start`, `period_end` | the time the estimate *describes* | | **Source release** | `source_release` | the upstream edition that *published* it | | **Catalog validity** | `valid_from`, `valid_to` | when Catchment Lake first/last carried this version of the row | ## A real example: PLACES 2024 vs. 2025 ::: {#7e2cda1e .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
source_release period_start period_end value valid_from valid_to
0 2024 2022 2022 6.5 2026.09 None
1 2025 2023 2023 6.6 2026.09 None
``` ::: ::: Two rows, same measure, same county (Denver County, CO). The **source release** is `'2024'` or `'2025'` — the PLACES edition. The **period** each release actually describes is one year *earlier*: the 2024 release models 2022 BRFSS data, the 2025 release models 2023 data. A query that filters on `source_release = '2025'` expecting "2025 data" is filtering on the release label, not the period — the value it gets describes 2023. `valid_from` is `'2026.09'` on both rows and `valid_to` is `NULL` on both: this is a bootstrap catalog, so every row so far carries the same catalog release. The catalog-validity axis becomes visible starting at the next catalog release that changes or retires a row — at that point `valid_to` stops being `NULL` on the superseded version, and a query for "what the lake said as of release 2026.09" becomes a real, answerable filter rather than a trivial one. ## A second example: an edition's own period moves SVI's `source_release` **is** the edition, and each edition's own period is a five-year ACS window that moves with it — never the edition year alone: ::: {#4f87f120 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
edition period_start period_end
0 2014 2010 2014
1 2016 2012 2016
2 2018 2014 2018
3 2020 2016 2020
4 2022 2018 2022
``` ::: ::: The 2020 edition's period is `2016`–`2020`, not `'2020'` alone — treating an edition's release year as its period would be off by up to four years. ## Why this matters for a catchment report The sentence a cancer center has to defend — *"in our catchment, as reported by source S in release R, the measure was X"* — names the release, not the period, on purpose: the release is what you can point back to when someone asks "where did this number come from." Reproducing a past analysis means filtering on `source_release`, not on `period_start`/`period_end` (a later release can restate an earlier period with revised numbers) and not on `valid_from`/`valid_to` (which tracks the lake's own history, not the source's).
